metadata.title: ICT and Digital Reading Achievement: A Cross-national Comparison using PISA 2018 Data

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for three countries (United States, Singapore, Finland) and analyzes students nested within schools. In the analytic plan, the authors state that both student- and school-level weights and clusters were implemented to account for PISA design effects, and they use Stata survey (svy) commands for estimation. The paper does not report the exact PISA weight variable names (e.g., student weight codes), so the specific weight variable cannot be extracted, but the presence of “student- and school-level weights” implies complex survey weighting was applied. Because the dependent variable is based on PISA reading achievement with plausible values, the weighted multilevel modeling is intended to produce population-representative associations while respecting the clustered sampling structure.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample includes PISA 2018 15-year-old students from the United States, Singapore, and Finland. The authors report that the final analysis sample sizes (USA: 3,645; Singapore: 6,090; Finland: 4,352) were obtained due to missing data in the variables used, implying listwise deletion/exclusion of cases with missing values on the focal variables and covariates. No additional grade or school-type restrictions are described beyond PISA’s standard sampling of schools and students.

confounders_identified.variable_name: Age of first digital device use
Availability of digital devices at home
Frequency of reading on digital devices

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (digital context), cross-national (USA, SGP, FIN)
main_findings.target_variable: Digital reading achievement (PISA reading achievement plausible values)
top_predictors: Frequency of reading on digital devices
Availability of digital devices at home
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel linear models (separate by country): Frequency of using digital devices → decreased achievement (USA B=-25.23, SE=5.65, p<.001; SGP B=-21.83, SE=2.33, p<.001; FIN B=-27.42, SE=3.53, p<.001). Attitude toward digital devices → increased achievement (USA B=20.22, SE=4.47, p<.001; SGP B=9.83, SE=2.49, p<.001; FIN B=20.09, SE=2.84, p<.001). Frequency of reading on digital devices → increased achievement (USA B=8.72, SE=4.29, p<.001; SGP B=12.80, SE=2.92, p<.001; FIN B=22.41, SE=3.17, p<.001). Gender interactions: Attitude×Female negative in USA (B=-10.19, SE=5.19, p<.05) and FIN (B=-11.09, SE=4.14, p<.01); Reading-on-digital×Female negative in SGP (B=-12.74, SE=4.66, p<.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (digital context) the study leveraged frequency of using digital devices, attitude toward digital devices, and frequency of reading on digital devices (with ESCS and home ICT availability as covariates) to analyze digital reading achievement, finding that general digital device use was negatively associated with achievement while both digital reading frequency and digital device attitude were positively associated. This indicates that policies and classroom/parent guidance should differentiate between “digital use for reading” and “general screen use,” and should strengthen students’ positive attitudes and reading routines on digital platforms to support digital reading achievement, while recognizing that gender moderation varies by country.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 reading achievement in a digital context for three countries (United States, Singapore, Finland), using ten plausible values for reading achievement and multilevel linear models to account for students nested within schools. The final analytic samples were USA N=3,645, Singapore N=6,090, and Finland N=4,352 after excluding cases with missing values on variables used. Across all three education systems, students’ attitude toward digital devices was positively associated with digital reading achievement (e.g., USA B=20.22, p<.001; SGP B=9.83, p<.001; FIN B=20.09, p<.001), while frequency of using digital devices was negatively associated (e.g., USA B=-25.23, p<.001). Frequency of reading on digital devices showed a positive association with achievement in all countries (e.g., FIN B=22.41, p<.001). Gender moderation was present for some relationships (attitude effects in USA/Finland; reading-frequency effect in Singapore). The paper does not use ML algorithms; therefore, results are correlational/associational rather than predictive-model performance.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction sets ml_techniques to empty because the paper reports multilevel linear models (with survey weights and clusters) rather than training/evaluating machine learning algorithms. Consequently, there are no ML model names, hyperparameters, or ML performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC) to extract. The study is still empirical and uses PISA plausible values, but its analytic strategy is conventional multilevel regression with interactions, not ML prediction.
